query: Single-phase fcc FeCoNi has high saturation magnetization but a low coercive field, and reported single-phase fcc high-entropy alloys derived from it have coercive fields no greater than 100 Oe in the reported magnetic measurements. What single intervention could overcome this coercivity limitation? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, the predicted change relative to single-phase fcc FeCoNi or a matched derivative, the relevant compositional, structural, and measurement boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled experiment with an explicit falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a small amount of Sn to the single-phase fcc FeCoNi alloy will induce the formation of a controlled dual-phase microstructure (fcc with dispersed BCC regions) that enhances domain wall pinning and consequently increases the coercive field well above 100 Oe.
generation.material_initial_state: Single-phase face-centered cubic (fcc) FeCoNi or a closely related HEA derivative with low coercivity (≈100 Oe) and high saturation magnetization.
generation.intervention: Introduce a minor alloying addition of Sn (on the order of a few atomic percent) into the FeCoNi base alloy.
generation.conditions: The alloy should be processed (e.g., via arc-melting and homogenization) under conditions similar to those used in prior studies, measured at room temperature, and with compositions possibly including minor CuAl additions if needed to stabilize the microstructure.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a dual-phase microstructure with predominantly fcc matrix containing well-dispersed BCC regions or precipitates.
generation.mechanism: The dispersed BCC phase acts as pinning centers for magnetic domain walls, impeding their motion under applied magnetic fields. This enhanced domain wall pinning increases the coercive field without significantly compromising the high saturation magnetization characteristic of the FeCoNi system.
generation.predicted_outcome: An increase in the coercive field relative to the single-phase fcc FeCoNi baseline (i.e., significantly exceeding 100 Oe), while retaining high saturation magnetization.
generation.baseline: Single-phase fcc FeCoNi or its matched derivative, which shows a coercive field of no greater than 100 Oe under similar processing and measurement conditions.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies to FeCoNi-based alloys processed under similar thermal and casting conditions as in the supporting studies, measured at or near room temperature, and where the Sn addition does not lead to excessive phase instability or formation of unwanted intermetallic compounds.
generation.uncertainty: The quantitative increase in coercivity is uncertain; while prior evidence in analogous systems suggests a significant enhancement, the precise magnitude and the optimal Sn concentration require experimental optimization.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of FeCoNi-based alloy samples with varying minor Sn concentrations (e.g., 0%, 2%, 5%, and 10% atomic Sn). Characterize the microstructure using X-ray diffraction and electron microscopy to confirm the emergence of a dual-phase (fcc/BCC) structure. Measure the magnetic hysteresis loops at room temperature to determine the coercive fields.
measurements: X-ray diffraction patterns to detect the presence of both fcc and BCC phases
Electron microscopy to observe the distribution and morphology of BCC precipitates
Magnetic hysteresis measurements to assess changes in coercive field and saturation magnetization
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the addition of Sn does not lead to the formation of a dual-phase microstructure or if, despite the structural change, the coercive field remains at or below approximately 100 Oe (i.e., no significant increase is observed relative to the single-phase baseline), then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: The present work exhibits the effects of Sn addition on the magnetic properties and microstructure of FeCoNi(CuAl)0.8Snx (0 ≤ x ≤ 0.10) high-entropy alloys (HEAs). The results show all the samples consist of a mixed structure of face-centered-cubic (FCC) phase and body-centered-cubic (BCC) phase. The addition of Sn promotes the formation of BCC phase, and it also affects the shape of Cu-rich nano-precipitates in BCC matrix. It also shows that the Curie temperatures (Tc) of the FCC phase and the saturation magnetization (Ms) of the FeCoNi(CuAl)0.8Snx (0 ≤ x ≤ 0.10) HEAs increase greatly while the remanence (Br) decreases after the addition of Sn into FeCoNi(CuAl)0.8 HEA. The thermomagnetic curves indicate that the phases of the FeCoNi(CuAl)0.8Snx (0 ≤ x ≤ 0.10) HEAs will transform from FCC with low Tc to BCC phase with high Tc at temperature of 600–700 K. This work provides a new idea for FeCoNi(CuAl)0.8Snx (0 ≤ x ≤ 0.10) HEAs for their potential application as soft magnets to be used at high temperatures.

In this work, the FeCoNi(CuAl)0.8Snx (0 ≤ x ≤ 0.10) HEAs were prepared by vacuum arc-melt casting. Effects of Sn content on the phase constitution and magnetic properties were studied. All the samples are composed of FCC and BCC phases, whereas some unknown phases appear with the addition of Sn. The addition of Sn promotes the formation of BCC phase, and it also affects the shape of Cu-rich nanoprecipitates in the BCC matrix. Moreover, the Ms increases greatly while the remanence (Br) decreases with the increasing of x for FeCoNi(CuAl)0.8Snx (0 ≤ x ≤ 0.10) HEAs. The addition of Sn can obviously increase the Curie temperature of the FCC phase. The phase of alloys with a mixture of FCC and BCC will transform from FCC to BCC phase at high temperature, leading to an increase of magnetization. They can be used as new soft magnetic materials at high temperatures.

reading.lever: Introduce a minor alloying element (e.g., Sn) to achieve a controlled dual-phase (FCC/BCC) microstructure that pins domain walls.
reading.why: Evidence shows that dual-phase structures yield higher coercivity through domain wall pinning, and Sn addition has been successfully applied in a related system.
